item.title: Intangible Assets on the Balance Sheet: Recognition, Amortization and Disclosure
item.summary: Intangible assets are valuable resources with no physical form, such as patents, licenses and software. This lesson covers when they appear on the balance sheet, how their cost is spread over time, and what the notes must reveal, because these rules change reported profit and asset totals.

sections.heading: What counts as an intangible asset
sections.body_markdown:
An **intangible asset** is a *nonmonetary* resource with *no physical substance* that is expected to bring future benefits. Examples are patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses, customer lists and software. Think of a restaurant franchise agreement: you cannot touch it, but it earns money for years.

To go on the balance sheet, an item must be **identifiable**, meaning it can be separated from the business or arises from a legal or contractual right. It must also be probable that it will bring future economic benefits, and its cost must be measurable reliably. **Goodwill** is a different item. It is the unidentifiable leftover paid in a business purchase, and it is covered in a separate lesson. Some costs, such as start-up costs, are never capitalized as intangibles.

Software that is built into a machine and needed to run it is usually folded into the cost of that equipment and reported as property, plant and equipment, not as an intangible.

sections.heading: How an intangible gets on the balance sheet
sections.body_markdown:
**Capitalizing** a cost means recording it as an asset and spreading it over later years, rather than **expensing** it, which means charging it all to profit now. There are three routes to recognition.

1. **Bought separately.** The asset is recorded at cost: the purchase price plus costs needed to get it ready for use, such as legal fees directly attributable to it.
2. **Acquired in a business combination.** Identifiable intangibles of the target are recognized at fair value. Whatever is left of the price is goodwill.
3. **Developed internally.** Most internally generated intangibles (a home-grown brand, customer relationships, advertising) are *not* recognized. Their costs are expensed. Internal **research-phase** costs are expensed under both IFRS and US GAAP.

The main difference is **development** costs, which are the work done after research to turn findings into a usable product. Under IFRS they are capitalized once specific criteria are shown, including technical and economic feasibility, intent to complete the asset, and ability to use or sell it. Under US GAAP they are generally expensed, with exceptions for software. Software built to be sold is capitalized after technological feasibility is established. Internal-use software is capitalized only for costs in the application development stage. Advertising and promotion costs are expensed under IFRS as incurred.

sections.heading: After recognition: amortization, revaluation and impairment
sections.body_markdown:
**Finite-life** intangibles have a limited period of expected benefit. Their cost is spread over their estimated useful life by **amortization**, which is the intangible-asset version of depreciation. Straight-line is common. Management must review useful life and method, and changes are treated as a *change in estimate*, applied going forward only (prior years are not restated).

**Indefinite-life** intangibles have no foreseeable limit on the period of cash inflows. They are *not amortized* but are tested for impairment at least annually, and sooner if there are warning signs. Note that "indefinite" does not mean "infinite".

**Impairment** means the asset's carrying amount is no longer supportable, so it is written down and a loss is recorded. IFRS uses a one-step test: if there are indicators, compare carrying amount with the **recoverable amount** (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use). US GAAP first checks recoverability using undiscounted cash flows, and only if that fails measures the loss against fair value. IFRS allows reversal of an impairment loss for intangibles other than goodwill, capped at what the carrying amount would have been without the loss. US GAAP does not allow reversals.

**Revaluation** to fair value is not allowed under US GAAP. IFRS permits it as a policy for a whole class of intangibles, but only where an active market exists for that type of asset, which makes it rare.

sections.heading: Disclosures and what an analyst should do with them

worked_example.problem: On 1 January, a company buys a software license from a vendor for $380,000 and pays $20,000 of legal fees directly needed to make the license ready for use. The license is expected to generate benefits for 5 years, with no residual value. The company uses straight-line amortization. What is the annual amortization expense?
steps: Identify the asset: a separately acquired license is an intangible with a finite life, so it is capitalized at cost and amortized.
Compute capitalized cost: purchase price plus directly attributable costs = $380,000 + $20,000 = $400,000.
Use the useful life (5 years), not any longer legal term, and a residual value of $0.
BA II Plus: press 400000 ÷ 5 = and read 80,000.
Check: after 2 years, accumulated amortization is $160,000 and carrying amount is $240,000.

formulas.name: Straight-line amortization
formulas.where: Cost is the capitalized cost of the intangible; Residual value is the expected value at the end of its life (usually zero for intangibles); Useful life is the estimated years of benefit.

formulas.name: Carrying amount
formulas.where: CA is the book value reported on the balance sheet; accumulated amounts are totals to date.

formulas.name: IFRS impairment loss
formulas.latex: \text{Loss} = \text{CA} - \text{Recoverable amount},\quad \text{Recoverable amount} = \max(\text{FV less costs of disposal},\ \text{Value in use})
formulas.where: CA is the carrying amount; FV is fair value; Value in use is the present value of cash flows from using the asset. A loss exists only if CA exceeds the recoverable amount.

exam_traps: Treating goodwill as just another amortizing intangible. It is a separate item and not amortized under IFRS or US GAAP for public companies.
Assuming development costs are treated the same way everywhere: IFRS capitalizes them when criteria are met, while US GAAP generally expenses them (software has exceptions).
Using the legal life of a patent or license instead of its estimated useful economic life when computing amortization.
Believing indefinite-life intangibles are never tested. They are not amortized but must be tested for impairment at least annually.
Forgetting that IFRS allows reversal of impairment losses on intangibles other than goodwill, while US GAAP prohibits all reversals.

item.stem: Which of the following costs is expensed as incurred under both IFRS and US GAAP, rather than recognized as an intangible asset?

options.text: Price paid to another company for a patent it owns
options.explanation: A separately purchased patent is capitalized at cost under both frameworks, so this is not expensed.

options.text: Internal costs of the research phase of a project
options.explanation: Correct. Research-phase costs do not meet the recognition criteria under either framework, so they are expensed as incurred.

options.text: Cost of a license bought separately for five years of use
options.explanation: A separately acquired license with probable future benefits and a reliable cost is capitalized and amortized.

item.stem: Which statement about development costs for an internally developed product (other than special software rules) is most accurate?

options.text: US GAAP capitalizes all development costs as incurred, while IFRS requires all of them to be expensed.
options.explanation: This reverses the frameworks. IFRS is the one that allows capitalization once criteria are met.

options.text: Both frameworks require every development cost to be expensed, with no exceptions in any circumstance.
options.explanation: IFRS capitalizes development costs when feasibility criteria are demonstrated, and US GAAP has software exceptions.

options.text: IFRS capitalizes them once criteria such as technical feasibility and intent to complete are met; US GAAP generally expenses them.
options.explanation: Correct. IFRS requires capitalization when the specific criteria are demonstrated. US GAAP generally expenses development costs unless another topic, such as certain software guidance, applies.

item.stem: A company buys a patent for $720,000. The patent has a legal life of 12 years, but the company expects it to generate cash inflows for only 8 years, after which it will be worthless. The company uses straight-line amortization and a residual value of zero. What is the annual amortization expense?

options.explanation: Correct. Cost of $720,000 minus zero residual, divided by the 8-year estimated useful life, gives $90,000.
Divides by the 12-year legal life instead of the 8-year expected useful life.
Treats the patent as indefinite-lived and does not amortize it, even though its benefits are expected to end after 8 years.

item.stem: An intangible asset has no foreseeable limit on the period over which it is expected to generate net cash inflows. How is it treated after recognition?

options.text: It is not amortized, but it is tested for impairment at least annually and when indicators appear.
options.explanation: Correct. Indefinite-life intangibles are not amortized and are tested for impairment at least yearly under both IFRS and US GAAP.

options.text: It is amortized over its legal life and is exempt from impairment testing once amortization begins.
options.explanation: Indefinite-life assets are not amortized, and no asset is exempt from impairment tests.

options.text: It is not amortized and is exempt from impairment testing because it has no useful life to measure.
options.explanation: Confuses no amortization with no testing. Indefinite-life intangibles must be tested at least annually.

item.stem: Which statement about revaluing intangible assets (other than goodwill) to fair value is correct?

options.text: It is permitted under both IFRS and US GAAP for any intangible asset at management's discretion.
options.explanation: US GAAP does not permit revaluation, and IFRS limits it to classes with an active market.

options.text: It is permitted under US GAAP for intangibles, but IFRS prohibits it because IFRS requires the cost model.
options.explanation: This reverses the frameworks. IFRS allows revaluation as a policy; US GAAP does not.

options.text: It is permitted under IFRS only as a policy for a class with an active market, and not under US GAAP.
options.explanation: Correct. IFRS permits revaluation for a class of intangibles when an active market exists, which is rare. US GAAP prohibits it.

item.stem: Two otherwise identical companies reporting under IFRS each pay 100 in cash in Year 1 to develop a new product. Firm A meets every IAS 38 criterion for capitalizing development costs and capitalizes the 100. Firm B expenses the 100. Assume Year 1 amortization on Firm A's new asset is small and ignore taxes. Compared with Firm B in Year 1, Firm A reports:

options.text: lower net income, the same operating cash flow, and higher total assets.
options.explanation: Treats capitalization as if it reduced profit. Capitalizing moves most of the 100 onto the balance sheet, so only a small amortization charge hits Year 1 income, and net income is higher than Firm B's. It also overlooks the cash flow classification.

options.text: higher net income, higher operating cash flow, and higher total assets.
options.explanation: Correct. Firm A defers most of the cost to the balance sheet and recognizes only a small amortization charge, so net income and total assets are higher. Its cash outflow for the capitalized development cost is classified as investing, whereas Firm B's expensed cost reduces operating cash flow by 100. So Firm A's operating cash flow is higher.

options.text: higher net income, the same operating cash flow, and higher total assets.
options.explanation: Reasons that both firms paid 100 in cash, so operating cash flow must match. The cash paid is the same, but its classification differs. Firm B's expensed 100 is an operating outflow, while Firm A's capitalized 100 is an investing outflow.

issues: solver chose C (high): Capitalizing 100 with small amortization gives higher Year 1 net income and total assets; the spending moves to investing cash flow, so operating cash flow is higher for A, not the same. Re-check: expensing in B reduces CFO by 100, while A reports it in CFO investing, so A's CFO is higher. Of the options, B says higher NI and higher CFO, which is correct.

item.stem: A company recognized an impairment loss on a finite-life intangible asset (not goodwill), and its estimated recoverable amount later rises. Which statement about reversing the loss is correct?

options.text: IFRS permits reversal, capped at the carrying amount that would have existed without the loss; US GAAP prohibits reversal.
options.explanation: Correct. IFRS requires review for reversal indicators and allows reversal up to the capped amount for assets other than goodwill. US GAAP does not permit reversals.

options.text: US GAAP permits reversal when fair value recovers, while IFRS prohibits all reversals of impairment losses.
options.explanation: Reverses the frameworks. IFRS is the one that permits reversal for non-goodwill assets.

options.text: Both frameworks permit full reversal of all impairment losses, including those on goodwill, without any cap.
options.explanation: Goodwill impairment can never be reversed, and IFRS reversals are capped.

item.stem: Which description best matches the note disclosures normally expected for intangible assets?

options.text: Only the closing net carrying amount in total, with no breakdown by class and no information on amortization.
options.explanation: Notes break out classes and show amortization methods, lives and movements, not just a single total.

options.text: By class: measurement basis, amortization methods and lives, opening and closing cost and accumulated amortization, and whether internally generated.
options.explanation: Correct. These class-level details, along with finite or indefinite life status and impairment losses, let analysts see how assets were built and written off.

options.text: For each class: the fair value at year-end, even when the cost model is used, with no cost or amortization details.
options.explanation: Under the cost model the disclosures focus on cost, accumulated amortization and movements, not a year-end fair value in place of those details.

item.front: How are finite-life and indefinite-life intangible assets treated differently after recognition?
item.back: Finite-life: amortized over estimated useful life. Indefinite-life: not amortized, but tested for impairment at least annually (and when indicators exist).

item.front: Research vs development costs for internally developed intangibles: how do IFRS and US GAAP treat them?
item.back: Research costs are expensed under both. Development costs are capitalized under IFRS once criteria (technical feasibility, intent to complete, ability to use or sell) are met; US GAAP generally expenses them, with software exceptions.

item.front: Can intangible assets be revalued to fair value?
item.back: US GAAP: no. IFRS: allowed as a policy for a whole class, but only with an active market for that type of asset, so it is rare.

item.front: Can an impairment loss on an intangible asset be reversed?
item.back: IFRS: yes for assets other than goodwill, capped at the carrying amount that would have existed without the loss. US GAAP: no.

item.front: What effect does capitalizing development costs (vs expensing them) have in the year of spending?
item.back: Higher net income, higher total assets and higher operating cash flow, because the outflow is classified as investing instead of operating.

warnings: 1/7 items have the longest option as the key
